blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Landslide susceptibility models are trained on inventories that record where landslides were seen, not where they occurred. The established remedy fits bias-describing variables and neutralises them when mapping. We adapt occupancy-detection modelling from ecology, treating several inventories as imperfect observers of one event and separating occurrence from recording, and ask when this improves on neutralisation. We use near-complete inventories of the 2018 Hokkaido Eastern Iburi, 2015 Gorkha and 2010 Haiti earthquakes with simulated reporting bias, and three real Gorkha inventories. Compared with standard practice, the occupancy model reduces road bias in 24 of 25 paired draws and raises AUC by 0.08-0.14 on Gorkha and 0.03 on Haiti, but only 0.01-0.02 on Iburi. Its median predicted-to-true landslide rate is 0.99 (range 0.44-1.89), against 0.24-0.30 for the baselines. Rescaling the baselines with the same anchor area corrects their median but leaves larger errors (range 0.20-4.34). Cell-level probabilities remain too extreme (calibration slope 0.59). Compared with the best neutralised model, AUC is higher on Iburi (by 0.03-0.07) and lower on Gorkha and Haiti (by 0.01-0.05). Transplant experiments tie the Iburi advantage to the structure of its true landslide pattern, not to its terrain or road network. In all eight settings with a low interaction gap, computable from biased records, neutralisation was at least as accurate, including a prespecified test on Haiti; a high gap did not guarantee an advantage. The real Gorkha inventories are slope-biased, not road-biased, and there the model brings no meaningful gain. Report-based catalogues remain the main untested case.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Data-driven landslide susceptibility maps depend on the inventories they learn from [ 1 ] . An
inventory is a record of observation: a landslide enters it when someone reports, surveys or maps it. Reporting is
easier near roads and towns and under clear skies, so inventories are spatially incomplete in systematic ways [ 2 , 3 ] . A classifier trained on such records learns the observation process together with
the hazard. The problem matters because landslides do not cluster near roads in the way reports do. In all three
earthquakes studied here, cells with mapped landslides lie farther from public roads than other cells (median 0.50
vs 0.25 km in Iburi, 0.66 vs 0.33 km in Gorkha, 0.81 vs 0.62 km in Haiti), so road-biased records under-sample
terrain where landslides are common.

blocks.en:
Dropping bias-related predictors confounds the remaining effects [ 2 ] . The established alternative
is to include them during fitting and remove their influence when mapping [ 4 ] . This neutralisation
needs only one inventory, but it assumes that the bias variables can be separated from the hazard signal inside a
single model. Ecology has long faced the same problem, since species are recorded where observers look. Occupancy
models address it structurally, with one process for true presence and another for detection, identified through
repeated surveys [ 5 ] . Several independently produced inventories of one event could play the role
of those surveys, but this requires more data than neutralisation, and whether it is worth the cost is an open
question.

blocks.en:
This paper therefore asks when treating inventories as imperfect observers improves on neutralisation. We make three
contributions: 1. A model. We adapt deep occupancy–detection modelling to landslide inventories, using separate
inventories of one event as repeated surveys, sign-constrained detection, and a small exhaustively mapped
anchor area. 2. An evaluation against a known reference. On real terrain, roads and near-complete inventories from
three earthquakes with simulated reporting bias, the model reduces road bias relative to standard practice
and estimates the overall landslide rate more stably than baselines, including baselines rescaled with the
same anchor. Its ranking advantage over neutralisation is confined to one earthquake. On three real Gorkha
inventories, whose bias follows slope rather than roads, it brings no meaningful gain. 3. An explanation and a selection rule. Transplant experiments link the ranking advantage to the
structure of the true landslide pattern rather than to terrain or roads. From this we derive a rule that can
be computed from biased records. In our tests a low value always meant that the simpler neutralisation
sufficed, including a prediction recorded before testing on a third earthquake. A high value is necessary
but not sufficient for an advantage.

blocks.en: 2 Related work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Statistical susceptibility models are reviewed by Reichenbach et al. [1] . Three lines of work show that inventory
bias changes model results. Steger et al. [2] introduced synthetic biases and showed that excluding bias-describing
predictors confounds the remaining effects, while mixed-effects models were least affected. Stanley and Kirschbaum [6] truncated a synthetic inventory to mimic road and population reporting biases and found that the effects should not
be ignored. In Bavaria, gaps in the inventory led to underestimated hazard in poorly mapped areas [ 7 ] . How bias arises depends on how an inventory was made. Field, report and newspaper inventories
under-sample terrain poorly visible from roads [ 3 ] , whereas excess landslide density near roads
appeared in only 3 of 12 inventories examined by Malamud et al. [8] , who attributed it to mapping remit. As remedies, Steger et al. [4] and Lima et al. [9] account for data-collection effects during fitting and remove them for
prediction, the latter at national scale. Steger et al. [4] enter bias-describing variables as random effects in a
generalised additive mixed model and zero them for prediction. In their South Tyrol case this bias-adjusted model had
limited success (median AUROC 0.59–0.61), which they attribute partly to test data that share the bias. These remedies
use one inventory and one model of the combined process, which is the assumption we examine.

A large literature treats bias as a problem of choosing non-landslide samples, for example positive–unlabelled
learning with adaptive sampling [ 10 ] or with a contrastive loss [ 11 ] . These methods address
unknown negatives, but not spatially structured under-reporting of positives.

Independent inventories of the Gorkha earthquake differ substantially in completeness and delineation [ 12 ] , and co-seismic inventories worldwide vary widely in quality and completeness [ 13 ] .

event are available, but they have rarely been used jointly in model fitting.

certain [ 19 ] . To our knowledge, occupancy modelling has not been applied to landslide inventories.

All models are trained and tested on spatial blocks of the same event, using epicentral distance as a feature. The

forecasts for a future earthquake.

blocks.en:
Terrain features come from the Copernicus GLO-30 surface model [ 33 ] , computed at 30 m and aggregated:
elevation, mean, maximum and standard deviation of slope, aspect, curvature, topographic position at 150 m and 600 m,
relative height, relief, and epicentral distance. GLO-30 derives from TanDEM-X data acquired between December 2010 and
January 2015. It therefore pre-dates Iburi and largely pre-dates Gorkha, but post-dates Haiti, where some landslide
scars may affect the terrain features. Observation features are distance to major roads, public roads and tracks [ 34 ] and built-up density (ESA WorldCover 2021, class 50 only) [ 35 ] . Other WorldCover classes
are excluded because they show landslide scars. Roads and built-up land also post-date all three events, so post-event
reconstruction is a limitation, chiefly for the real-inventory test. In the simulations the same fields define detection,
so the mismatch does not arise. No shaking variable is used: epicentral distance is a proxy for shaking.

Three real Gorkha inventories from the USGS ground-failure repository [ 14 ] are used without simulation.
Their coverage is the convex hull of each inventory within the window. The anchor area is taken from the reference
inventory, so the model sees about 2% of the reference. Models are scored against the reference and against a consensus
(a cell in at least 2 of the 4 inventories). The consensus includes the training records, so it is not an independent
test, and it can favour models fitted to them.

blocks.en:
Standard practice is one MLP trained on the union of all records, including anchor records, with terrain and
access features. Standard, roads dropped uses terrain features only. Neutralised models are fitted to the
same union with access features, which are then set to their mean for prediction. We implement this as an MLP, a logistic
GLM and a generalised additive model (GAM) with cubic splines. Steger et al. [4] instead use a generalised additive mixed model with
bias variables as random effects, zeroed for prediction. We follow the same logic, but with access features as fixed effects.
In the additive GLM and GAM, a constant access value gives the same ranking as zeroing those terms, but the fitted
coefficients differ because no random-effect shrinkage is applied. Our results therefore evaluate neutralisation in these
three model classes, not the mixed-model method itself. Where we refer to the best neutralised
model, we take the highest AUC among the variants on each draw, which favours neutralisation because the best variant
cannot be known in practice. The oracle is an MLP trained on the reference inventory.

Spatial blocks of 25 × 25 25\times 25 cells are split 60/15/25 into training, validation and test sets. Test-block metrics are

bias is | log ⁡ R | |\log R| . The oracle’s road bias (0.11–0.45) indicates the noise floor of this metric. For probabilities we
report the ratio of mean predicted to true rate, expected calibration error (ECE; 10 equal-frequency bins), log loss, Brier
score and calibration slope (the coefficient from a logistic regression of outcomes on predicted log-odds; 1 is ideal, and
values below 1 mean predictions are too extreme). Each setting has five random draws of the reporting realisation,
split and anchor. Comparisons within a scenario are paired on identical draws, using counts and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [ 36 ] . Splits differ between scenarios A and C, so we do not compare results across them. With five draws a
two-sided test cannot go below p = 0.0625 p=0.0625 , and draws within an earthquake share terrain and truth, so we report site-level

blocks.en: 6 Discussion
blocks.zh: 讨论

blocks.en:
Both approaches remove much of the road-driven reporting bias, but they have different costs and strengths. Neutralisation needs one inventory and, where susceptibility is close to additive, it ranks
at least as well. The occupancy model needs at least two inventories with different biases and a small exhaustively mapped area. In return it estimates the overall rate more stably and, in some settings,
ranks better. We suggest the following procedure. Fit a gradient-boosting and an additive model to the available records and compute the interaction gap on held-out blocks. If the gap is below 0.015,
use neutralisation for ranking, since nothing in our tests favoured the extra data requirement. If it is larger, the occupancy model may help, but this is not assured. In either case, if the overall
rate matters and an anchor area exists, the occupancy model gave more stable rates than scaling a neutralised model.
blocks.zh:
这两种方法都消除了道路驱动的报告偏向,但它们的成本和长处不同。 中立需要一份清单,如果易感性接近添加剂,则需要排行
至少也一样。 入住模式至少需要两份有不同偏见的库存清单,并有一个细小的、详尽无遗的区域。 作为回报,它估计总的费率比较稳定,而且在某些情况下,
排好一点 我们建议采用以下程序。 将梯度起动和添加型号与现有记录相匹配,并计算被搁置区块的相互作用差距。 如果差距低于0.015,

blocks.en:
Neither generic nonlinearity nor road-proxied signal explains the Iburi advantage; the combination of epicentral structure and interactions in the real pattern does. One reading is that a flexible
neutralised model fits part of that structure through the road variables, and discards it when they are neutralised. Slope is more strongly correlated with road distance on Iburi ( r = 0.50 r=0.50 – 0.59 0.59 for
public and major roads) than on Gorkha ( 0.39 0.39 ) or Haiti ( 0.23 0.23 – 0.37 0.37 ), which is consistent with this reading. It is not established, however: terrain as a whole predicts road distance better on
Gorkha than on Iburi ( R 2 R^{2} 0.74 vs 0.49), and a GLM loses on Iburi for a simpler reason, as it cannot represent interactions at all. We avoid describing this as a shaking × \times terrain interaction, since we measured epicentral distance and not shaking. Testing the role of shaking directly, for example with USGS ShakeMap, is a natural next step.

blocks.en:
The method was designed for reporting driven by roads and population, and the real inventories we could test have a different kind of bias. This fits earlier observations that road effects depend on how an
inventory is made [ 8 ] : satellite mapping of a whole event has no need to follow roads. Slope bias is harder, because slope also drives real occurrence, which undermines the exclusion
restriction. On such inventories, a standard terrain-only model is already within 0.016 AUC of the oracle, leaving little room for improvement. Scoring against a near-complete reference also matters for all these comparisons: Steger et al. [4] note that performance measured on biased test data can understate a bias-adjusted model. Our results do not show that the method is useful on real
inventories, only that it does not fail on ranking; for rate estimation and slope bias it was worse than the alternatives.

blocks.en: 7 Conclusions
blocks.zh: 7 结论

blocks.en:
Treating several biased landslide inventories as imperfect observers reduces simulated road and population bias relative to standard practice and gives more stable estimates of the overall landslide rate than
baselines, including baselines rescaled with the same anchor area, although cell-level probabilities remain too extreme. Whether it also ranks better than neutralisation depends on the structure of the true
landslide pattern: it did on Iburi, but not on Gorkha or Haiti. Wherever the interaction gap computed from biased records alone was low, neutralisation was at least as accurate, including a
prediction recorded before testing on Haiti, whereas a high gap did not guarantee an advantage. On real satellite-mapped inventories, whose bias follows slope and not roads, the model brought no meaningful gain.
Neutralisation remains the sensible default for ranking when only one inventory exists or the interaction gap is low. The case for the occupancy model rests on rate estimation and on patterns with strong
interactions, and its value on the report-based catalogues it was designed for is still to be shown.
